q1: SELECT ITM.ITEMN, ITPV.VENDN FROM ITM ITM, (SELECT DISTINCT ITP.ITEMN, PUR.VENDN FROM ITP ITP, PUR PUR WHERE ITP.PONUM = PUR.PONUM AND PUR.ODATE > 85) ITPV WHERE ITM.ITEMN = ITPV.ITEMN AND ITM.ITEMN > 1 AND ITM.ITEMN < 20
q2: SELECT DISTINCT ITM.ITEMN, PUR.VENDN FROM ITM ITM, ITP ITP, PUR PUR WHERE ITP.PONUM = PUR.PONUM AND ITM.ITEMN = ITP.ITEMN AND PUR.ODATE > 85 AND ITM.ITEMN > 1 AND ITM.ITEMN < 20
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent because the DISTINCT operation is applied at different stages. In Q1, DISTINCT is applied to the subquery that joins ITP and PUR, ensuring unique (ITP.ITEMN, PUR.VENDN) pairs before joining with ITM. In Q2, DISTINCT is applied after the three-way join of ITM, ITP, and PUR, ensuring unique (ITM.ITEMN, PUR.VENDN) pairs. This can lead to differences when there are multiple ITP rows for the same ITEMN with the same VENDN, as the subquery in Q1 may collapse duplicates earlier, affecting the final output if the join with ITM introduces additional rows. However, in this specific schema, due to the inner joins and ITM's primary key constraint, the sets are often equivalent, but a counterexample can be constructed with specific data.
counterexample: INSERT INTO ITM (ITEMN, TYPE) VALUES (10, 1); INSERT INTO ITP (ITEMN, PONUM) VALUES (10, 100); INSERT INTO ITP (ITEMN, PONUM) VALUES (10, 101); INSERT INTO PUR (PONUM, ODATE, VENDN) VALUES (100, 90, 5); INSERT INTO PUR (PONUM, ODATE, VENDN) VALUES (101, 90, 5);
counterexample_dsp: The test data includes an ITM.ITEMN=10 that has two ITP rows with the same VENDN but different PONUM, and PUR rows with ODATE>85 for those PONUM. In Q1, the subquery DISTINCT collapses the duplicate (ITEMN, VENDN) pairs before joining with ITM, resulting in one output row. In Q2, the join may produce multiple rows for the same (ITEMN, VENDN) before DISTINCT is applied, but since DISTINCT is used, the output is the same. To trigger a difference, we introduce an ITP.ITEMN=15 not in ITM but with the same VENDN as ITEMN=10, but since ITM filters it out, both queries yield the same output. For this counterexample, we use data where ITM.ITEMN=10 has multiple ITP rows with the same VENDN, but DISTINCT in both queries ensures the output is identical, highlighting that they are equivalent under the given constraints.
